titre: The Cult Born of American Materiel
accroche: In 1942, the American army sets up its bases in a Pacific archipelago. A movement that began before it finds confirmation there.
contenu_vulgarise:
1942. In the archipelago then called the New Hebrides, today Vanuatu, American forces land to establish military bases, in the Pacific War. On the neighboring island of Espiritu Santo, more than 500,000 service members would pass through the naval base in all, and nine million metric tons of materiel would be shipped there, according to Wikipedia's article on that base. On the island of Tanna, this deployment landed in an already charged context: since the late 1930s, people there had been talking about John Frum.

## A Prophet Who Announces American Aid

According to the anthropologist Lamont Lindstrom, who did most of his fieldwork on Tanna, John Frum is an enigmatic figure who appeared in the late 1930s. He asked his followers to return to their original lands, to resume drinking kava and dancing, and to maintain island custom, *kastom*. Presbyterian missionaries had tried to ban kava; the followers rejected this prohibition. John Frum also predicted American material aid, which seemed to come true in 1942 with the arrival of the bases. The colonial authorities, for their part, imprisoned leaders of the movement, to little effect. As early as 1941, according to the anthropologist Marc Tabani, repeated signs of a large-scale rebellion appeared on Tanna, and the British administration accumulated thousands of pages of surveillance notes in order to suppress this political-religious movement.

The leaders invented rituals that blend Christian liturgy with the experience of war: marches, drills, flags, poles, flowers. On February 15, 1957, they raised two red flags recovered from American ammunition depots. That date remains the movement's main annual festival.

## More Than a Naive Belief

The expression “cargo cult” commonly designates a belief judged irrational. Lindstrom points out, however, that this label is often considered misleading: criticized as an observer's category that lumps together very diverse movements, it has been abandoned by many anthropologists. He lists competing readings: greed, Melanesian cultural and religious beliefs, spiritual salvation, psychological explanations, relative deprivation, or a reaction to colonial inequality and oppression. In this last family, Jean Guiart saw in these cults “forerunners of Melanesian nationalism” (1951), and Peter Worsley saw movements that unite scattered local groups into “new unities.”

The meaning of the word “cargo” itself evolved on Tanna, according to Lindstrom: first a synonym for money and new goods, it ended up designating local autonomy, then economic development projects. In his view, the John Frum movement is no longer a cargo cult: it has become institutionalized as an indigenous church and a political organization. What the arrival of the Americans in 1942 confirmed, then, was not a passive wait for merchandise, but a lasting organization that continues to exist.

carte.punch: The American bases of 1942 seem to confirm a prophet announced as early as the late 1930s.
carte.idee: In 1942, American forces establish bases in the archipelago, which seems to confirm the prediction of American material aid attributed to John Frum, who appeared on Tanna in the late 1930s. The movement has since become institutionalized as a church and a political organization.

quiz.question: What reading of these movements does Lamont Lindstrom attribute to the ethnologist Jean Guiart?
choix: As a precursor of Melanesian nationalism, born of colonial conditions that had become unbearable
As a mere imitation, without understanding, of the symbols of Western modernity
As a fraud organized by a few leaders to capture humanitarian aid
As a survival of religious beliefs predating any colonial contact
quiz.explication: Lindstrom cites Jean Guiart (1951), for whom cargo cults are “forerunners of Melanesian nationalism,” within a review of several interpretations (colonialism, cultural beliefs, spiritual salvation, etc.). Neither an imitation without understanding, nor an organized fraud, nor a survival predating colonial contact is Guiart's reading.

quiz_supplementaire.question: What happened on February 15, 1957, a date that remains the John Frum movement's great annual festival?
choix: Leaders raised two red flags recovered from American ammunition depots
The prophet John Frum officially returned to the island of Tanna
The colonial administration legally recognized the John Frum movement
The New Hebrides gained independence under the name Vanuatu
quiz_supplementaire.explication: On February 15, 1957, leaders of the movement raised two red flags recovered from American ammunition depots, according to Lindstrom; that date remains the main annual festival.

quiz_supplementaire.question: According to the anthropologist Marc Tabani, what did the British administration accumulate about the John Frum movement starting in 1941?
choix: Documentary films shot on the island
Thousands of pages of surveillance notes and reports
Treaties signed with the movement's leaders
A few letters that went nowhere
quiz_supplementaire.explication: Faced with repeated signs of a large-scale rebellion that appeared on Tanna in 1941, the British administration accumulated, in order to suppress this political-religious movement, thousands of pages of surveillance notes, reports, and commentary (Tabani, Paideuma, 2018).

quiz_supplementaire.question: How did the meaning of the word “cargo” evolve over time, according to Lindstrom?
choix: It designated only American military aircraft from the start
From material goods toward local autonomy, then development led by the islanders
It has never changed meaning since 1942
It ended up designating only tourists visiting the island
quiz_supplementaire.explication: According to Lindstrom, the word cargo, at first a synonym for material goods and new money, came to designate local autonomy, then economic development projects carried out by the islanders themselves.
